newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian central bank officials discuss the baht.
newsitem.headline: Asian central bank officials discuss the baht.

text.p: Asian central bank officials met in Bangkok on Saturday and the top item on their agenda was the recent speculative attack against the Thai baht, central bank sources said on Sunday.

The Bank of Thailand issued a one paragraph statement about the meeting which read in part, "The meeting has contributed to strengthening the cooperation among the central banks and monetary authorities in the region and enhancing the stability of the regional financial markets."
But foreign exchange traders contacted by Reuters said it was obvious the main topic of conversation amongst the officials would have been the Thai baht.

"The meeting would have been a post mortem about the events of the week before last. They'll have looked at what they did right and what they did wrong," the head of foreign exchange trading at a European bank in Singapore commented.
A central bank offcial from one of the banks attending the meeting declined to specifically say what had been discussed, but added, "Look at the timing and draw your own conclusion."

On May 14 and 15 the baht was the subject of a massive attack by speculators who had decided that the combination of a high current account deficit, economic woes and rumours of instability in the cabinet were good reasons to sell the baht.
The Bank of Thailand -- with the aid of other Asian central banks -- was able to fend off the attack.

Since the so-called 'Tequila Crisis' of 1994 when the Mexican peso was savaged by speculators, Asian central banks have been signing bilateral repurhase pacts between each other in which they agree to help defend their currencies against speculative attacks.
The first real test of these repurchase pacts came with the foreign exchange market's assault against the baht.

The usually secretive Monetary Authority of Singapore confirmed it had intervened to defend the baht while the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, although not confirming it officially, was also highly visible in intervening.
The Thai central bank said this weekend's gathering was part of the regular meeting of the Executives' Meeting of East Asia and Pacific (EMAP) Central Banks.
But the head of trading at the European bank said, "Regular it may be, but the location is a bit of a coincidence. They're sending a message to the speculators."
He added, "The message is pretty simple. It's along the lines of 'You're not taking Thailand on, you're taking all of us on.'"
The meeting was attended by senior central bank officials from Japan, Singapore, Malaysia, South Korea, Indonesia, China, Hong Kong and Thailand.

The head of Treasury at a U.S. bank in Singapore told Reuters he had not been aware of Saturday's meeting. "I think its hugely significant. They may say its under the auspices of EMAP, but...they would, wouldn't they."
"A lot these (central) bankers are worried that what happens to Thailand today could happen to them tomorrow. This sort of gathering of the clans will give them confidence," he added.
